div.p: Energy efficiency is a critical design constraint in multicore Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS). Using energy management methods can violate timing constraints; hence, designing scheduling policies that can adapt to the dynamic and unpredictable nature of aperiodic real-time tasks remains a significant challenge. This paper introduces LEETMIC, a novel deep reinforcement learning framework for energy-aware realtime scheduling. To manage a variable number of active jobs, LEETMIC utilizes a learned policy network to determine the scheduling priority and Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling (DVFS) level for each task individually, based on a combination of the task's local attributes and a summary of the global system state. The policy is trained using Multi-Agent Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (MADDPG) algorithm to co-optimize for both task schedulability and energy consumption. The trained policy neural network is a compact multi-layer perceptron (MLP), making it suitable for online deployment in embedded systems. Experimental results demonstrate that, compared to the Global Earliest Deadline First (GEDF) scheduler, LEETMIC achieves a similar success ratio while significantly reducing energy consumption by 41.5% on average (up to 70%).

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Cyber-Physical Systems (CPSs) drive modern technologies, from autonomous vehicles to robotics and wearable devices [1]. While the multicore processors foundational to these systems unlock complex application capabilities, they inherently have a critical energy-performance trade-off, which is a significant concern for battery-powered platforms [2]. Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling (DVFS) attempts to manage this by tuning processor power, but lower settings inevitably increase execution times, pushing systems toward real-time deadline violations. Consequently, the central challenge lies in designing scheduling algorithms that can simultaneously optimize the conflicting objectives of energy efficiency and schedulability.

Traditional scheduling algorithms, whether using fixed or dynamic priorities, struggle when faced with the complexity of multicore platforms and the unpredictability of aperiodic tasks [3]. Simple fixed-priority models offer ease of implementation but lack the flexibility for dynamic workloads, while dynamicpriority methods gain adaptability at the cost of significantly higher computational overhead. Reinforcement Learning (RL) presents a powerful paradigm for optimal decision-making under uncertainty, yet its application in scheduling remains focused on narrow subproblems. Existing RL work primarily tackles limited scenarios, such as optimizing power consumption exclusively for periodic tasks [4] or scheduling aperiodic tasks without energy considerations [3]. This leaves energyaware scheduling for unpredictable and dynamic workloads on multicore systems less explored. Conventional RL algorithms are not well-suited to address this complex problem effectively. Hence, this paper addresses this gap by proposing LEETMIC, a multi-agent deep reinforcement learning framework for energy-efficient, preemptive priority-driven scheduling. LEETMIC is dynamically scalable; it assigns priority and determines the execution frequency for each incoming job individually. This is achieved via a multiagent setting where the agent uses a fixed-size summary of the global state instead of complete details about jobs, and the reward function is designed to balance energy efficiency and schedulability. Furthermore, the approach explores frequency scaling as a continuous variable during training before transitioning to discrete voltage-frequency scales when online.

To motivate our approach, Fig. 1 compares the performance of LEETMIC against GEDF, which prioritizes schedulability by continuously operating at maximum frequency, and Energy-Saving DVFS (ES-DVFS) [5], a greedy heuristic that minimizes energy by always selecting the lowest feasible frequency. The results, averaged across experiments on 4core, 8-core, and 16-core systems with per-core utilizations of 0.25, 0.5, and 0.75, show that LEETMIC achieves a success ratio of 98.2% (comparable to GEDF's 99.8%) while reducing energy consumption by 41.5% compared to GEDF. In contrast, ES-DVFS achieves only a 76.8% success ratio, which is undesirable, despite its lower energy consumption. This highlights LEETMIC's superior trade-off between schedulability and energy efficiency.

The main contributions of this work are as follows: (i) A novel RL for dynamic, energy-aware scheduling of aperiodic real-time tasks on multicore processors, (ii) A state and action representation that combines local instance information with global system statistics to facilitate effective collaborative policy learning, (iii) Empirical evaluations demonstrating that the learned policy can reduce energy consumption compared to conventional schedulers without compromising schedulability.

div.head: II. SYSTEM MODEL AND PRELIMINARIES
div.p: This section formally defines the system architecture, task model, and energy model used in this work.

div.head: A. Platform and Application Model
div.p: The hardware platform consists of a multicore processor with M identical (homogeneous) cores, P C = {P C 1 , P C 2 , . . . , P C M }, each supporting independent dynamic voltage and frequency scaling. To focus on the highlevel scheduling policy, we assume the cores are fully connected and that the cost of inter-core communication is incorporated into each job's execution time, making it negligible from the scheduler's perspective.

The application consists of N aperiodic firm real-time tasks, T = {T 1 , . . . , T N }, each generating a sequence of task instances, known as jobs. As our focus is on dynamic scheduling of aperiodic tasks, we consider the set of independent active jobs that have been released but not yet completed, denoted by J = {J 1 , J 2 , . . . , J N ′ }, where N ′ is the number of active jobs at a given time. Each job J i ∈ J is defined by

where A i is the arrival time (or release time) of the job, c i > 0 is the Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET) at the maximum frequency f max , and d i ≥ c i is the relative deadline. From these parameters, we define the absolute deadline of job J i as
div.formula: D i = A i + d i .
div.p: The state of an active job J i at time t is tracked by its remaining execution time, C i (t), starting at
div.formula: C i (A i ) = c i . A job is considered complete at time F i when C i (t) = 0 for t ≥ F i , meeting its deadline if F i ≤ D i . A deadline miss occurs if t > D i and C i (t) > 0.
div.p: As tasks are firm real-time, a single miss does not cause catastrophic failure, though our goal is to minimize missed jobs. As the tasks are aperiodic, job arrivals are not known in advance, and the scheduler operates online. Also, Jobs are independent, do not share any resources other than the processor cores, and can be preempted at any time and resumed later on any available core without incurring a time penalty.

div.head: B. Power and Energy Model
div.p: The power consumption within a modern processor core is primarily composed of static power and dynamic power. To manage energy consumption, we utilize DVFS. We assume a near-linear relationship between voltage and frequency, allowing them to be scaled by a common factor ρ m ∈ (0, 1]. By using these, the total power of a core m at time t, P m total (t), is expressed as a function of its scaling factor ρ m as shown in Eq. 1 [6], where ρ m (t) is the scale factor of core m at time t, set to a minimum value when idle or determined by the scheduler for executing active jobs. Also, the total energy consumed to successfully execute job J i on core m, E i (ρ m ), is calculated as Eq. 1 [6], where the total time required to complete its entire workload c i at a constant scaling factor ρ m is extended to ci ρm .
div.formula: P m total (t) = ρ m (t)P max static + ρ 3 m (t)P max dynamic , E i (ρ m ) = (P max static + ρ 2 m P max dynamic )c i .
div.p: This model establishes the fundamental trade-off between task execution time and energy consumption, which is central to our energy-efficient scheduling problem.

div.head: III. PROPOSED METHOD
div.p: This section presents the proposed method for energyaware real-time scheduling using RL. We first describe the RL framework, followed by the formulation of the state, action, and reward components. Finally, we outline the training procedure for the RL-based scheduling algorithm. LEETMIC is visualized in Fig. 2 A. Reinforcement Learning Framework

We model the scheduling problem as a Markov Decision Process (MDP), where agents interact with the environment in discrete time steps, observing state S t , taking action A t , transitioning to state S t+1 , and receiving reward r t . The goal is to learn a policy that maximizes the expected cumulative reward, balancing energy efficiency and schedulability. To handle a varying number of jobs, we utilize the Multi-Agent Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (MADDPG) algorithm [7] with centralized training and decentralized execution. Each active job is assigned a homogeneous agent. The global state S t is decomposed into local observations s i t per agent i, combining job-specific details with fixed-size global system statistics. This allows each agent to make decisions based on its own context while being aware of the broader system. Each agent i selects action a i t = (α i , ρ i ), where α i is the job's priority and ρ i is the voltage-frequency scale, using a shared policy network parameterized by θ π . The global action A t = {a 1 t , . . . , a N ′ t } determines scheduling decisions, selecting the M highest-priority jobs for execution on an Mcore system, each with its corresponding scaling factor.

A critic network, parameterized by θ Q , estimates individual Q-values Q i (s i t , a i t |θ Q ) for each agent i, predicting the future reward for action a i t in state s i t . The global Q-function is the average of these Q-values, forming the centralized critic:
div.formula: Q(S t , a 1 t , . . . , a N t ) = 1 N ′ N ′ i=1 Q i (s i t , a i t |θ Q ).(2)
div.p: This addresses credit assignment by considering individual contributions to the global reward. The critic is trained by minimizing the mean-squared Bellman error, which compares the predicted Q-value to a target value computed using a target critic network and the reward r t . The target critic network, parameterized by θ Q ′ , is a slowly updated copy of the critic, which provides more consistent target values to stabilize training. The shared policy network is trained using policy gradients, with the critic's Q-values optimized to maximize the expected cumulative reward. The overall policy outputs priorities and scaling factors for N ′ active jobs, {J 1 , . . . , J N ′ } → {(α 1 , ρ 1 ), . . . , (α N ′ , ρ N ′ )}, enabling scalable scheduling across varying number of active jobs.

div.head: B. State, Action, and Reward Function
div.p: Each agent i 's state combines local attributes of job J i (e.g., relative deadline, remaining execution time) with global system statistics (e.g., minimum, maximum, and average of deadlines, execution times, and slack times of active jobs). This global information helps agents cooperate, reducing voltage-frequency scaling during low system load and enabling them to focus on completing all jobs rather than just their own.

Each agent i outputs an action a i = (α i , ρ i ), where α i is the priority of job J i and ρ i ∈ (0, 1] is the voltage-frequency scaling factor for its execution. The system schedules the M highest-priority jobs on an M -core system at their specified ρ i . The remaining execution time of job J i is updated as c i (t + 1) = c i (t) -ρ i , if executed. A job is removed from active set when c i (t) = 0 or deadline is reached (d i = t). To maintain training stability in MADDPG, continuous values for ρ i are used during training. However, since processor voltagefrequency scaling is usually restricted to discrete levels, the continuous ρ i is mapped to the nearest ceiling discrete during online inference.

The reward function is designed to align with the objectives of energy-aware real-time scheduling, which are to maximize the number of jobs that meet their deadlines while minimizing energy consumption. At each time step t, the reward function is defined as
div.formula: r t = λ s |SJ t | -λ m |M J t | -λ e E t ,
div.p: where |SJ t | is the number of jobs that complete and meet their deadlines at time t, |M J t | is the number of jobs that miss their deadlines, and E t is the processor's energy consumption at time t. The coefficients λ s ≥ 0, λ m > 0, and λ e > 0 balance the trade-off between maximizing the success ratio and minimizing energy consumption. Through extensive empirical evaluation, we set λ s = 0 to prevent agents from prioritizing early job completion for immediate rewards, which could lead to excessive energy consumption due to the conflicting nature of these goals. This approach promotes energy-efficient scheduling policies. λ m > 0 and λ e > 0 are determined based on system specification.

div.head: C. Algorithm Discussion
div.p: The training procedure for our scheduler agent is outlined in Algorithm 1. It runs for a fixed number of episodes (line 4). Each episode starts by resetting the environment (line 5). In each time step, every agent i selects an action a i t = π(s i t |θ π ) + noise (line 9), where noise is sampled uniformly from an interval defined by a noise width parameter. This noise width decreases exponentially over episodes, shifting from exploration to exploitation (line 23). The global action A t = {a 1 t , . . . , a N ′ t }, where N ′ is the number of active jobs, is executed, yielding the reward r t and next state S t+1 (lines 12). The transition (S t , A t , r t , S t+1 ) is stored in a replay buffer (line 13). For learning, a minibatch of size B is randomly sampled from the replay buffer to train the networks (line 14). The critic network, parameterized by θ Q , is trained by minimizing the Bellman loss using target Q-values computed via the target policy and critic networks with parameters θ Q ′ and θ π ′ (line 15). The actor network, parameterized by θ π , is trained using the policy gradient method, leveraging the critic's Q-values to optimize the policy (line 16). Target networks (θ π ′ , θ Q ′ ) are softly updated to ensure training stability (line 17). If the episode terminates, the loop exits, and metrics such as success ratio and energy are recorded (lines 18-22).

div.head: IV. EXPERIMENTS
div.p: To assess the performance of the proposed approach for energy-aware real-time scheduling, LEETMIC, we conducted experiments using synthetically generated task sets in a simulation environment. Task sets were generated to simulate diverse workloads with varying characteristics, which is essential to train and evaluate the RL agent on thousands of scenarios and ensure its policy generalization. To achieve a target average system utilization, we first used Stafford's Randfixedsum algorithm [8] to generate a set of base task utilizations (u i ). For each task, the relative deadline d i was sampled from a log-uniform distribution over the range [10, 100]. The tasks are aperiodic, with job arrivals for each task T i following a Poisson process. This was achieved by sampling job interarrival times from an exponential distribution with a mean equal to the task's deadline, d i . The execution time for each task, c i , was then calculated as the product of its base utilization and its deadline (c i = u i d i ). This generation process simulates a scenario with aperiodic tasks, where job arrivals are entirely random and the system has no prior knowledge of future workloads. Consequently, while the long-term average system utilization, computed as the total execution time of jobs arriving over a sufficiently long time interval divided by the interval length, aligns with the target utilization set by the Randfixedsum algorithm, the instantaneous load at any given moment can vary significantly. This approach allows us to evaluate the scheduler's robustness and adaptability to the dynamic and unpredictable nature of real-world aperiodic workloads.

To ensure low online overhead, the shared policy network is implemented as a compact Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with two hidden layers (16 and 8 neurons). The critic network, which is only used during offline training, is a similarly small MLP (two hidden layers with 32 and 12 neurons). The performance of LEETMIC is evaluated against GEDF, an optimal scheduling algorithm adapted to aperiodic jobs, and ES-DVFS, a greedy energy-saving baseline that selects the lowest frequency ensuring deadline feasibility, assuming no interference. Prior RL-based works [3], [4] are not directly comparable as they target different system models which cannot be trivially extended. The primary performance metrics are the success ratio, defined as the percentage of jobs that complete before their deadline, and the normalized energy consumption. For the GEDF baseline, all cores operate at maximum frequency, and energies are normalized relative to GEDF.

Fig. 3-a shows performance across per-core utilizations (0.2 to 0.7) on a 4-core system. LEETMIC reduces energy by 39.0% on average with a 97.9% success ratio, close to GEDF's 99.8%. ES-DVFS reduces energy consumption by 75.7%, but its success ratio drops to 72.9%, prioritizing energy over potential future job interference. Fig. 3-b assesses scalability across 4 to 16 cores at a per-core average utilization of 0.5 (increasing tasks proportional to the number of cores).

LEETMIC achieves a 37.1% energy reduction and 99.4% success ratio, achieving a much better trade-off than ES-DVFS's 68.7% energy reduction but 79.8% success ratio. Fig. 3-c evaluates varying task counts (12 to 44) on a 4-core system at per-core utilization of 0.5. LEETMIC maintains a 99.5% success ratio, near GEDF's 100%, with 40.1% less energy. ES-DVFS reduces energy by 81.6% but achieves only 69.4% success ratio. Overall, when averaged across 4 to 16 cores and per-core utilizations ranging from 0.25 to 0.75, LEETMIC achieves a success ratio of 98.2% while reducing energy consumption by 41.5%.

These results demonstrate LEETMIC's ability to balance energy efficiency and schedulability across diverse utilizations, core counts, and task sets, closely matching GEDF's success ratio while having significant energy savings.

V. CONCLUSION This paper presents LEETMIC, a multi-agent deep reinforcement learning framework for energy-aware scheduling of aperiodic real-time jobs on multicore CPSs. Experimental results demonstrate that LEETMIC reduces energy consumption by 41.5% compared to GEDF while maintaining success ratio, significantly outperforming greedy baselines like ES-DVFS.
